title: Peaks, pits and saddles
objectives: Find the stationary points of a function of two variables.
Recognise a peak, a pit and a saddle on a contour map.

screens.title: Level ground
screens.prose: A contour map of hilly ground. Each curve joins points of equal height. Blue curves are above sea level, amber curves below it, and purple is sea level.

state.caption: Contours every 0.5 m. One grid unit is 1 km.

screens.question: Tap every lettered point where the ground is level in every direction.

hints.text: Where could you take a small step any way without climbing or dropping?
Look where the curves close into small rings, and where two curves cross.
C and F sit inside closed rings: a summit and a hollow. A and G sit where the sea-level curves cross: two passes.

feedback.correct: A summit, a hollow and two passes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Level points sit inside the smallest rings or where two curves cross.

byKey.rings-only: You found the summit and the hollow. At A and G two curves cross: those are passes, and a pass is level too.
byKey.A: You left out A, where two sea-level curves cross. Walking through A, one way climbs and one way falls, but A itself is level.
byKey.G: You left out G, where two sea-level curves cross. G is a pass between two hills, and the ground there is level.
byKey.B: B sits between rings, on a slope. Walking east from B you climb towards the summit at C.
byKey.D: D is on the sea-level curve, but the ground still slopes there. Being on a contour does not make a point level.
byKey.E: E is on the side of the hill round C. Walking west from E you climb.

explain.text: You picked the points with no slope at all. Rings close round the summit C and the hollow F. At the passes A and G two contours cross, so the ground rises one way and falls the other.

canvas.caption: Level ground: a peak C, a pit F and passes A and G

screens.title: Where the arrow vanishes
screens.prose: The map is $f(x, y) = \sin x + \sin y$. The arrow at P is the gradient $\nabla f = (\cos x, \cos y)$, drawn at half length. Drag P around.
screens.question: Drag P onto the summit, the hollow and each pass. What is true of $\nabla f$ at all of them?

options.text: Both components are 0, so the arrow vanishes
One component is 0 and the other is not
options.why: That happens along a whole line, such as $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. At the four level points both read 0 together.

options.text: It points straight up the steepest slope
options.why: That is true on a slope. At the summit there is no uphill direction left, so the arrow has nothing to point at.
On a slope the gradient crosses the contours at right angles. At the level points it has shrunk to nothing.

hints.text: Drag P onto C and read the caption.
The summit and the passes all sit at $x = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $y = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, where cosine is 0.

feedback.correct: At every level point the gradient is the zero vector.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag P onto the summit and read both numbers in the caption.

explain.text: You saw the arrow shrink to nothing at the summit, the hollow and both passes. There $\cos x = 0$ and $\cos y = 0$, so $\nabla f = (0, 0)$. Points where the gradient vanishes are called **stationary points**.

screens.title: Solving for a stationary point
screens.prose: A stationary point is where $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$, so $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$ at once. Take $$f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 2x + 4y.$$ Solve both equations, then drag P there.
screens.question: Drag P to the stationary point.

hints.text: Differentiate with respect to $x$, holding $y$ fixed. Then the other way round.
$f_x = 2x - 2$ and $f_y = 2y + 4$. The caption shows both at P.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2x - 2 = 0$ and $2y + 4 = 0$, then place P there.

byKey.sign-y: You placed P at $y = 2$. From $2y + 4 = 0$, $y = -2$: the sign flips when the 4 moves across.
byKey.both-signs: Both signs flipped. $2x - 2 = 0$ gives $x = 1$, and $2y + 4 = 0$ gives $y = -2$.

explain.text: You solved $2x - 2 = 0$ and $2y + 4 = 0$ together and got $(1, -2)$. Both partials read 0 there, and the rings close round it. Each equation alone fixes only one coordinate; together they fix the point.

screens.title: More than one
screens.prose: Now take $$f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2.$$ Find every solution of $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$. The map shows its contours, with the level $f = 2$ in purple.
screens.question: Select all that apply: tap every stationary point.

hints.text: Write down $f_x$ and $f_y$ first.
$f_x = 3x^2 - 3$ and $f_y = 2y$. Points with $y \neq 0$ fail the second equation.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2y = 0$ and $3x^2 - 3 = 0$ together.

byKey.plus-only: You took only $x = 1$. The equation $x^2 = 1$ has two roots, so $(-1, 0)$ is stationary too.
byKey.one-partial: D and E make $f_x = 0$, but $f_y = 2y$ is not 0 there. Both partials must vanish.
byKey.D: At D, $f_x = 0$ but $f_y = 2$. The ground still slopes in the $y$ direction.
byKey.E: At E, $f_x = 0$ but $f_y = -2$. The ground still slopes in the $y$ direction.
byKey.C: C is where $f = 0$, not where the slope is 0. There $f_x = -3$.
byKey.F: F is where $f = 0$ on the $x$-axis. There $f_x = 3(3) - 3 = 6$, so it slopes.

explain.text: You solved $2y = 0$ first, then $3x^2 = 3$, which has two roots. Rings close round A, so A is a pit. The purple contours cross at B, so B is a saddle.

canvas.caption: A: rings close (a pit). B: contours cross (a saddle).

screens.title: A saddle
screens.prose: Take $f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2$. Here $f_x = 2x$ and $f_y = -2y$, so the only stationary point is $(0, 0)$. Blue contours have $f > 0$, amber $f < 0$, and purple $f = 0$.
screens.question: What does the ground do at $(0, 0)$?

options.text: It rises along the $x$-axis and falls along the $y$-axis
It is a pit, since $f = x^2$ rises either side along the $x$-axis
options.why: You walked along the $x$-axis only. Along the $y$-axis $f = -y^2$, which falls either side.

options.text: It is a peak, since $f = -y^2$ falls either side along the $y$-axis
options.why: You walked along the $y$-axis only. Along the $x$-axis $f = x^2$ rises.

options.text: It is not level, because $f$ takes negative values nearby
options.why: Negative heights do not make a slope. $\nabla f = (2x, -2y)$ is $(0, 0)$ at the origin.

hints.text: Walk along the $x$-axis through the origin, then along the $y$-axis.
On the $x$-axis $f = x^2$. On the $y$-axis $f = -y^2$.
One walk climbs either side, the other falls either side. The contours $f = 0$ cross at the origin.

feedback.correct: Up one way, down the other: a saddle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the walk along the $x$-axis with the walk along the $y$-axis.

explain.text: You compared two walks through the origin: one climbs, the other falls. A stationary point like that is a **saddle**, shaped like a horse's saddle or a mountain pass. On a contour map, the level curves cross there.

canvas.caption: The contours $f = 0$ are the lines $y = x$ and $y = -x$, crossing at the saddle.

screens.title: Only one equation
screens.prose: Find the stationary point of $$f(x, y) = x^2 - 2xy + 2y^2 - 2y.$$ Here $f_x = 2x - 2y$ and $f_y = 4y - 2x - 2$. The green line is where $f_x = 0$.
screens.question: Where is the stationary point?

options.why: You solved $f_x = 0$, got $x = y$, and picked $(0, 0)$ on that line. There $f_y = -2$, so the ground still slopes.
You set only $f_x$ to zero, which leaves a whole line. $f_y = 0$ must hold too, and its line cuts $y = x$ once.
You set $x = 0$ and solved $f_y = 0$ for $y$. But $f_x = -1$ at $(0, 0.5)$.

hints.text: The point must lie on the green line and also satisfy $f_y = 0$.
On the green line $x = y$. Put that into $f_y = 0$.
$4y - 2y - 2 = 0$ gives $y = 1$, and then $x = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $x = y$ from $f_x = 0$ inside $f_y = 0$.

byKey.line: You stopped after $f_x = 0$. That equation alone gives the whole line $y = x$; the second equation picks one point on it.
byKey.origin: $(0, 0)$ satisfies $f_x = 0$ only. A stationary point needs both partials to be zero.

explain.text: You substituted $x = y$ from the first equation into the second, giving $y = 1$. Each equation alone is a line of points. The stationary point is where the two lines cross.

screens.title: A flat valley floor
screens.prose: Take $f(x, y) = (x - y)^2$. Its contours are straight lines parallel to $y = x$. Work out $f_x$ and $f_y$ with the chain rule.
screens.question: How many stationary points does $f$ have?

options.why: You found one solution of $x - y = 0$ and stopped. $(2, 2)$ and $(-1, -1)$ make both partials 0 as well.

options.text: None: there is no single lowest point
options.why: You looked for one isolated point. The lowest value, 0, is reached all along $y = x$, and the ground is level there.

options.text: Infinitely many: every point on $y = x$

options.why: Each partial gives an equation, not a point. Here both equations say the same thing: $x = y$.

hints.text: Differentiate $(x - y)^2$ with respect to $x$, then with respect to $y$.
Both are zero exactly when $x = y$. That is a whole line of points.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2(x - y) = 0$ and $-2(x - y) = 0$ and count the solutions.

explain.text: You found that both partials are multiples of $x - y$. So both vanish at every point of $y = x$: a valley with a flat floor. Stationary points need not be isolated.

canvas.caption: Every point on the purple line is stationary.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Each time you solved two equations together. For a function of two variables, $$\nabla f = \mathbf{0} \iff f_x(x, y) = 0 \text{ and } f_y(x, y) = 0.$$ The solutions are the **stationary points**: peaks, pits, saddles, or whole lines of them.
screens.question: Which system gives the stationary points of $f = x^2 + xy + y^2$?

options.why: That is $f_x = 0$ only. It is a line; $f_y = 0$ cuts it down to points.
You dropped the $xy$ term. Its $x$-partial is $y$ and its $y$-partial is $x$.
That sets the height to zero. Stationary means the slope is zero.

hints.text: Differentiate each term, including $xy$.

feedback.correct: Both partials, set to zero together.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $f_x$ and $f_y$, keeping the $xy$ term.

explain.text: The $xy$ term gives $y$ in $f_x$ and $x$ in $f_y$. The system $2x + y = 0$, $x + 2y = 0$ has the single solution $(0, 0)$.

screens.title: Why the rings are centred there
screens.prose: We found $(1, -2)$ for $f = x^2 + y^2 - 2x + 4y$. Completing the square shows it is the lowest point, not just a level one.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $f = (x^2 - 2x) + (y^2 + 4y)$, group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms
$\geq -5$, since squares are never negative, with equality only at $(1, -2)$

hints.text: Start by sorting the terms by variable.
Group, complete both squares, collect $-1 - 4 = -5$, then use that squares are at least 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group by variable before completing the squares.

byKey.bound: The inequality needs the squares on show, so it comes last.
byKey.square: Group the terms by variable before you complete each square.

explain.text: Grouping, then completing both squares, writes $f$ as $(x - 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 - 5$. Each square is zero only at $(1, -2)$. The contours $f = c$ are circles of radius $\sqrt{c + 5}$ round that point.

screens.title: Sizing two strategies
screens.prose: A desk runs two strategies at sizes $x$ and $y$, in £m. Their trades overlap, so expected daily P&L, in £k, is $$P = 10x + 8y - x^2 - y^2 - xy.$$

state.caption: Contours of $P$ appear after you answer.

screens.question: At which sizes are both partial derivatives of $P$ zero?

options.why: You dropped the $-xy$ term: $10 - 2x = 0$ and $8 - 2y = 0$. The overlap pulls both sizes down.
You swapped the two answers. Check $P_x = 10 - 2x - y$ at $(2, 4)$: it is 2, not 0.
You solved $P_x = 0$ with $y = 0$ and ignored $P_y$. There $P_y = 8 - 0 - 5 = 3$.

hints.text: Write $P_x$ and $P_y$, keeping the $-xy$ term.
From the first, $y = 10 - 2x$. Then $8 - 2(10 - 2x) - x = 0$ gives $3x = 12$, so $x = 4$ and $y = 2$.

feedback.correct: £4m and £2m, for an expected £28k a day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $10 - 2x - y = 0$ and $8 - 2y - x = 0$ together.

explain.text: You solved the two linear equations together and got $(4, 2)$. There $P = 40 + 16 - 16 - 4 - 8 = 28$, so £28k a day. The rings close round it: whether it is a peak, we test next lesson.

ideas: A stationary point is where $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$: both partial derivatives vanish at once.
Contours close into rings round a peak or a pit, and cross at a saddle.
Solve $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$ as one system. The answer can be one point, several, or a whole line.

formula.name: Stationary points
formula.note: Two equations in two unknowns, solved together.

summary.trap: Setting only $f_x = 0$ gives a curve of points, not a point. The stationary points are where it meets $f_y = 0$.

options.why: You flipped both signs. $2x + 6 = 0$ gives $x = -3$.
You set $x + 6 = 0$, forgetting the 2 in $2x$.
At the origin $f_x = 6$ and $f_y = -8$, so the ground slopes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $f_x = 2x + 6$ and $f_y = 2y - 8$ to zero.

explain.text: $f_x = 2x + 6 = 0$ gives $x = -3$, and $f_y = 2y - 8 = 0$ gives $y = 4$. So the stationary point is $(-3, 4)$.

quiz.question: How many stationary points does $f$ have?

byKey.one: You took only $y = 1$. $y^2 = 1$ has two roots.
byKey.four: $x$ has only one value, $x = 0$, so there are $1 \times 2$ points.

explain.text: $f_x = 2x = 0$ forces $x = 0$. $f_y = -3y^2 + 3 = 0$ gives $y = \pm 1$. That is two points.

quiz.prose: On a contour map, two level curves cross at a point P, and P is a stationary point.
quiz.question: What kind of stationary point is P?

options.why: Contours close into rings round a peak. They do not cross there.
Contours close into rings round a pit too. Crossing curves mean up one way, down the other.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of $x^2 - y^2$ at the origin.

explain.text: Where two curves of one height cross, the ground climbs between one pair of arms and falls between the other. That is a saddle, as for $x^2 - y^2$ at the origin.

options.why: $(2, -1)$ also gives $x + 2y = 0$, so both partials vanish there too.
Both partials are multiples of $x + 2y$, which is zero along a whole line.

options.text: Every point on the line $y = x$
options.why: That was the valley of $(x - y)^2$. Here the bracket is $x + 2y$.

feedback.correct: A whole line of stationary points.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $f_x$ and $f_y$ with the chain rule.

explain.text: $f_x = 2(x + 2y)$ and $f_y = 4(x + 2y)$. Both vanish exactly when $x + 2y = 0$, a whole line.
